summary: A small upright desk box: a Sensirion SCD-40 photoacoustic CO2 sensor (Adafruit breakout) and a Raspberry Pi Pico on the back lid, a 0.96 in 128x64 OLED behind a window in the front, and a red/green bi-colour LED at the top of the front that fades from green through yellow to red as CO2 rises (green below 1000 ppm, red from 2000 ppm, the German UBA guide values). USB 5 V comes in through the Pico's own micro-USB socket on the right side. Everything runs at 3.3 V from the Pico; the sensor and the OLED share one I2C bus over a STEMMA QT cable; the firmware is CircuitPython.
architecture: Power: USB 5 V (phone charger or computer, micro-B cable) -> Pico VBUS -> Pico's on-board buck-boost -> 3V3(OUT), pin 36
3V3(OUT) -> SCD-40 breakout VIN (sensor power jumper left at its default, VIN) -> STEMMA QT cable -> OLED breakout V+ (its own regulator and charge pump)

I2C0: Pico GP4 (pin 6) = SDA, GP5 (pin 7) = SCL -> SCD-40 breakout SDA/SCL (10k pull-ups on the breakout) -> STEMMA QT -> OLED SDA/SCL; addresses 0x62 (SCD4x) and 0x3D or 0x3C (OLED, found by an I2C scan in code.py)

Light: Pico GP14 (pin 19) -> 390 ohm -> LED red anode; GP15 (pin 20) -> 390 ohm -> LED green anode; LED common cathode -> GND (pin 18); both pins PWM (slice 7, channels A and B) to mix green, yellow, orange and red
Ground: Pico GND pin 8 -> SCD-40 GND (and on through STEMMA QT to the OLED); Pico GND pin 18 -> LED cathode

Firmware: CircuitPython for the Pico with adafruit_scd4x, adafruit_displayio_ssd1306 and adafruit_display_text from the Adafruit CircuitPython bundle; code.py reads CO2, temperature and humidity every 5 s and sets the screen and the LED

Case: front shell (front wall, four side walls, four corner columns with M3 inserts) and a flat back lid, FDM PLA; the lid carries the Pico and the sensor, the shell carries the OLED and the LED; four M3 x 6 screws close it
assembly: Before you start. Tools: soldering iron (with a heat-set insert tip if you have one), solder, flush cutters, wire strippers for 26 AWG, a PH1 Phillips screwdriver for the M2 screws (TME gives PH1 for these DIN 7985 heads), a 2 mm hex key for the M3 button heads, a multimeter with a diode test (step 9), a hot-glue gun or a drop of superglue for the LED, 3 pieces of 2 mm heat-shrink about 15 mm long, and a computer with a USB port. Print the front shell and the back lid in PLA (black hides the LED's glow through the walls): front shell face down on the bed, lid flat, 0.2 mm layers, 4 perimeters (enough for the 2 mm walls) and 20 % infill; no supports are needed.

Flash the Pico first, on the bench. Hold BOOTSEL, plug the Pico into the computer, copy CircuitPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico (the .uf2 from circuitpython.org/board/raspberry_pi_pico) onto RPI-RP2, and wait for the CIRCUITPY drive. From the Adafruit CircuitPython bundle for that version, copy adafruit_scd4x.mpy, adafruit_displayio_ssd1306.mpy and the folders adafruit_display_text and adafruit_bus_device into CIRCUITPY/lib, then copy software/code.py (in this product's folder) to CIRCUITPY/code.py. Unplug.
Lay the front shell face down. Press the 4 M3 inserts into the 4 corner columns from the open back, flush with the rim, with the iron at the insert tip's temperature for PLA.
Push the bi-colour LED into the hole at the top of the front, from inside, until its flange sits on the wall. Fix it with a drop of hot glue on the flange.

Set the OLED in behind the window: glass toward the window, bottom edge on the printed ledge, its two upper holes on the two bosses. Fasten it with 2 M2 x 4 screws, finger tight (the glass must not be pressed hard).

Lay the lid inner face up. Set the Pico on its four 4 mm standoffs, components up, with the USB socket at the end that has two short printed pins: those two holes drop over the pins. Fasten the other end with 2 M2 x 6 screws (a pan head next to the USB socket would hit it, which is why that end has pins).

Fasten the CO2 sensor breakout (the order buys Adafruit's SCD-41 version, the same board as the SCD-40) on the lid's four tall standoffs with 2 M2 x 6 screws in the two diagonal standoffs that have holes: the sensor (the white square block) faces the lid, over the five vent slots, and the 5-pin header row is at the bottom, toward the Pico.
Wire the sensor: solder 4 pieces of 26 AWG wire, about 50 mm each, from the Pico to the SCD-40 header: pin 36 3V3(OUT) to VIN, pin 8 GND to GND, pin 7 GP5 to SCL, pin 6 GP4 to SDA.

Wire the light: with the multimeter's diode test, find the common cathode (the lead both colours light from, as the black probe) and which anode lights red. Bend all three leads 90 degrees toward the right side (the USB side) about 3 mm behind the flange: straight back they would hit the sensor's board, which sits 12 mm behind the LED once the lid is on, and to the right of that board, under the top, there is about 18 mm of free room. Solder a 390 ohm resistor to each anode there. Then about 80 mm of wire from the red resistor to Pico pin 19 (GP14), from the green resistor to pin 20 (GP15), and from the cathode to pin 18 (GND), slipping a piece of heat-shrink onto each wire before you solder it on at the LED end: shrink one over each resistor with both its joints and the third over the cathode's joint, so no bare lead can touch another.
Plug the 100 mm STEMMA QT cable into the SCD-40's right-hand connector and the OLED's right-hand connector.

Test before closing: plug the USB cable into the Pico and a charger or the computer. Within about 10 s the screen shows the CO2 in ppm, the temperature and the humidity, and the LED is green in a ventilated room. Breathe gently toward the vent slots: the CO2 rises and the LED moves toward yellow. If the screen stays blank, open the serial console (Mu or screen) and read the error code.py prints.

Close the case: unplug the USB cable, tuck the wires so none crosses the vent slots or the USB opening, set the lid on the shell with the Pico's USB socket at the side opening, and fasten 4 M3 x 6 screws into the inserts.
Stick the 4 rubber feet under the bottom, one near each corner.

Plug the USB cable into the Pico through the opening in the right side, and the other end into a phone charger or the computer. Set the monitor on the desk where you sit, not next to a window or your face.

Settle it in: leave it running for a day. The SCD40's self-calibration (on by default) needs fresh outdoor air (about 400 ppm) for at least 3 minutes once a week, so air the room now and then or set it on an open window sill for 5 minutes. To match the temperature to a thermometer next to it, change TEMP_OFFSET_C in code.py (the sensor's default is 4 C) and save.
estimates: co2BoardThicknessMm 1.2: Adafruit gives 7.7 mm overall for the SCD-40 breakout and the SCD4x datasheet 6.5 mm for the sensor; the board is taken as the difference. Measure it before printing the lid (it sets how far the sensor sits from its vents).
oledBoardThicknessMm 1.6 and oledTapeMm 0.1: Adafruit's usual board and a typical adhesive; not published. They set the OLED's two bosses (1.55 mm).
oledGlassCentreFromBottomMm 12.573: taken as the origin of the panel part U1 in Adafruit's board file; that the part's origin is the glass's centre is an assumption.

oledActiveFromGlassTopMm 2.1: read as an unlabelled '(2.1)' on the UG-2864HSWEG01 drawing as it came through as text; the window (24.4 x 13.5 mm) is 1.3 mm larger than the active area each way to absorb the error. Check the window against the panel on the first print.

Adafruit's product page for 326 gives the PCB as 29.2 x 26.7 mm; its board file (Adafruit 0.96in 128x64 OLED STEMMA QT.brd) is 29.21 x 31.75 mm with holes at 2.54/26.67 x 2.54/29.21. The design uses the board file. Measure the board when it arrives; a 26.7 mm board would have no upper holes to screw.
ledFlangeMm 5.8, ledFlangeThicknessMm 1.0, ledSeatedHeightMm 8.6 and ledDieAboveSeatMm 2.5: the usual Kingbright T-1 3/4 package; the WP59SURKCGKW pages read here give only '11.35 mm max height'.
jstBody* (6.0 x 4.25 x 2.95 mm): a JST SH 4-pin side-entry header as it sits on Adafruit's boards, from the pad layout in the board files; the body size is not in those files.

picoTallestAboveBoardMm 2.8, picoUsbCentreAboveBoardMm 1.35 and the micro-USB socket flush with the board's end: carried over from the keypad example's Pico numbers; the Pico datasheet's drawing gives the board, not the socket.
usbOvermoldWidthMm 11, usbOvermoldHeightMm 8: a typical micro-B cable's moulding; measure the cable you use (a bigger moulding will not reach the socket through the 12.5 x 9.5 mm opening).
picoBoardMa 30: the Pico running CircuitPython, an allowance; the Pico datasheet's figures are for its own test programs.

m2PilotMm 1.7: a pilot for an M2 machine screw to cut its own thread in PLA, from common practice; no maker publishes it. If the screws are loose, use a drop of glue; if they are too hard to turn, drill the holes to 1.8 mm.

sensorPortRadiusMm 2.5 and sensorPortMinOpen 0.4: the SCD4x's gas opening is on its top face, but the datasheet read here gives no size; the share is what five 1.6 mm slots on a 3 mm pitch can leave open, not a Sensirion figure.
cableTugN 0.3: a guess at the sideways pull of a USB cable lying on the desk; the stability check uses it.

Masses: the Pico (3 g), the LED (0.3 g), the resistors, screws, inserts, feet and cable are typical weights for those parts, not published figures; the SCD-40 breakout (2.8 g) and the OLED (4.5 g) are Adafruit's.
usbcable cordDiameterMm 3.5: a typical USB 2.0 cord, for the figure only; the USB-A shell (12.0 x 4.5 x 12 mm) is the USB 2.0 standard's.
costNotes: Currency and VAT: every shop prices in EUR; the quote's dollars are each shop's price without VAT, plus 22% Italian VAT, at 1.1253 USD/EUR (ECB, 2026-10-16). What you pay is the EUR total at each checkout, which may differ by a few percent (the shop's own VAT handling for Italy, rounding).

Prints: priced as filament only (36 g of PLA at the Sunlu spool's price), for a friend's printer. A spool, failed prints, supports and power are not counted. An online print service is not quoted: Sprue's print rate (Craftcloud) is a US figure, and a real quote needs the STL uploaded, which was not done.
Packs: the order buys 50 inserts, 100 of each screw and 4 feet for a unit that uses 4, 4, 4 + 2 and 4; the rest are spares.
Not in the total: solder, heat-shrink, a little hot glue, a heat-set insert tip if your iron has none, and a USB charger (any 5 V phone charger or the computer).
No customs or import duty: every shop in the order is in the EU. A UK shop (The Pi Hut, Pimoroni) would add DHL Express (GBP 30 at The Pi Hut) and EU import charges.
Free-shipping thresholds not reached: Opencircuit from EUR 150, BerryBase from EUR 250.
